sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Wsjr** ​(*osiris*) — ‌The Dead, ‌Resurrection, ​the Nile's ​Return ​· Mighty ​One — ​belongs ‌to the ​Egyptian ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Afterlife, ‌Resurrection, ​Vegetation". The ​name ​means "Mighty ​One (Egyptian ​wsjr)"[^1].

‌**Wsjr** — ​Osiris ‌to the ​Greeks — ‌is ​the god ‌who ​died and ‌returned, and ​in ​returning became ‌the pattern ‌every ‌Egyptian hoped ​to ​follow. Murdered ‌by his ​brother, ​reassembled by ‌his ​wife, enthroned ​as judge ‌of ​the dead, ‌he rules ​the ​*Duat* while ​his ​son Horus ‌rules the ‌living ​world above.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling ‌**Wsjr** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/osiris/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*osiris* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Hieroglyphs ​as **𓁥**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Mighty ​One (Egyptian ‌wsjr)"[^1].

The ​canonical ​spelling **Wsjr** ‌matches ​the conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ​*osiris* contains ​the same ​letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics or ‌encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. The ​editorial ‌work is ​to ‌fix one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ‌and ‌provenance, and ​keep the ​original ‌evidence visible. ​The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ​a description ‌computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **o** ‌→ ‌**W** — ​Initial w: ‌bilabial ​glide
- **s** ​→ ‌**s** — ‌Same
- **i** ‌→ ‌**j** — ​J: ‌palatal approximant
- ​**r** → ​**r** ​— Same
- ‌**i** ​→ **—** ​— ​Dropped: absorbed ‌in j
- ​**s** ​→ **—** ​— ‌Dropped: not ​in standard ‌translit

​Attested and ‌derived ​spellings of ‌the name:

- ‌**Osíris** ​— alternate ​stress, ​scholarly variant: ​Acute on ‌iota: ‌alternate stress ​position

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the name ​is ​**/ˈwɛzɪər/ ​(conventional)** ​— ‌Conventional ​reading ​— Egyptian ‌vocalisation ​not ‌attested.[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by ​phoneme:

- ​**Ws-** — ​The ​name ​is ‌written ​wsjr; ‌the ​initial ‌w is ​a ‌weak ​consonant ‌(w ​or ​u) ‌whose vowel ‌is ‌unwritten.
- ​**-jr** ​— ‌The ​god-determinative ​follows; the ‌final ​r ​is ‌consonantal. ​Egyptologists ‌conventionally ​vocalise ​the name ​“Wesir”.

​For ‌the ‌modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ​is: ‌“WES-ir” ‌— ‌the ‌form ​the ‌Greeks heard ​as ​Ὄσιρις ​(Ósiris)

‌Kindred ​and ​historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

- ​**Greek** ​— ‌Ósiris
- ​**Coptic** ‌— ​ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲉ (Ousire)

‌Egyptian ​hieroglyphs ‌record ‌consonants, ​not ​vowels; ​every vocalisation ​is ‌a ‌modern ​convention.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Wsjr** ​— Osiris ‌to ‌the ​Greeks — ​is ​the ​god who ​died ‌and returned, ​and ​in ‌returning became ​the ‌pattern ​every Egyptian ‌hoped ​to follow. ​Murdered ​by ​his brother, ​reassembled ‌by ​his wife, ‌enthroned ​as judge ‌of ​the ‌dead, he ​rules ‌the ​*Duat* while ​his ‌son Horus ‌rules ‌the ​living world ​above.[^1]

### ‌King ​of the ​Duat

‌Sovereign of ​the ​underworld ‌and judge ​of ‌every ​soul weighed ​against ​the feather ​of ‌Maat.

### ‌The First ​Mummy

‌The ​drowned, dismembered ​god ‌rewrapped by ‌Anubis ‌— ‌the prototype ​of ‌all ​mummification.

### The ​Green ​God

Lord ‌of ​vegetation ​and the ​inundation; ‌his ​green or ​black ​skin is ‌the ​fertile ‌flood-plain.

### Father ​of ‌Horus

​Posthumous father ‌of ‌the sky-falcon; ​the ​succession ​struggle with ​Seth ‌is ‌Egypt’s central ​myth.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Wsjr ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ‌set of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**King ​of ​the ‌Duat** ​— ‌Sovereign ​of ‌the underworld ​and ‌judge ​of ‌every ​soul ​weighed ‌against ‌the ‌feather ​of ​Maat.
- ‌**The ​First ​Mummy** ‌— ​The ​drowned, ‌dismembered god ​rewrapped ‌by ​Anubis ​— ​the ​prototype ‌of ‌all ​mummification.
- ‌**The ​Green ​God** ‌— ‌Lord ‌of ‌vegetation ​and ‌the inundation; ​his ​green ​or ‌black ​skin ​is ​the ‌fertile ​flood-plain.
- ​**Father ​of ‌Horus** ​— ‌Posthumous ​father ‌of ​the sky-falcon; ‌the ‌succession ​struggle ​with ​Seth ​is ‌Egypt’s ‌central ​myth.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The Osiris ​cycle is the best-preserved ‌Egyptian myth, known from ‌the Pyramid Texts ​onward: the good king ​murdered by his brother, ​the faithful wife ​who recovers him, the ​son who avenges him. ‌It is simultaneously ​a story about kingship, ​about the flood that ‌dies and returns, and ​about every human ‌being who hoped to ​be judged worthy.[^1]

### The ‌Death of the ​Good King (Pyramid Texts)

​The earliest sources already ​presuppose the story: ​Osiris ruled as a ​beneficent king until his ‌brother Seth, envious ​of his power, contrived ‌his death — in ​the classical telling ‌(Plutarch’s *De Iside et ​Osiride*, the fullest narrative ‌we have) sealed ​in a chest and ‌thrown into the Nile, ​the river carrying ​him to Byblos where ‌a tamarisk grew to ‌engulf the coffin.[^2]

### Isis ‌the Faithful (Plutarch)

​Isis searched for the ​body, recovered it from ‌Byblos, and hid ​it — but Seth ​found it by night, ‌cut it into ​fourteen pieces, and scattered ​them through Egypt. Isis ‌and Nephthys wandered ​the land gathering the ‌fragments. Every place that ​claimed a fragment ​became an Osiris sanctuary; ​the myth is a ​map of Egyptian ‌pilgrimage.

### The Weighing of ‌the Heart (Book of ​the Dead)

Anubis ‌conducts the dead to ​the Hall of Two ​Truths, where the heart ‌is set on ‌the scale against the ‌feather of Maat and ‌the tally is ​read aloud by Thoth. ‌Wsjr, enthroned in the ​next chamber, receives ​those who pass. The ​formula “I am Osiris” ‌in the Book ​of the Dead identifies ​the deceased with him ​— his resurrection ‌becomes the template of ​theirs.

### The Succession of ​Horus (Memphite Theology)

​Isis, by magic, conceived ‌a son on the ​briefly reanimated body: ‌Horus, raised in secret ​in the marshes of ‌Chemmis, who grew to ​challenge Seth for ‌the throne. The tribunal ‌of the gods awarded ​Egypt’s rule to ​Horus and the underworld’s ​to Osiris — the ​mythic charter for ‌the division between the ‌living king and his ​dead father.
